role: One of the Ten Promised Paradise
Early companion and participant in major battles
summary: Sa'id ibn Zayd (RA) was one of the Ten Companions promised Paradise. He was the son of Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, the remarkable pre-Islamic Makkan who rejected polytheism and sought the pure religion of Ibrahim (AS) before the advent of Islam. Sa'id accepted Islam early in the Makkan period through the influence of Umar ibn al-Khattab's sister Fatimah, who was his wife, and through his own search for truth inherited from his father.
biography:
Sa'id ibn Zayd al-Adawi al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 593 CE into the Banu Adi clan of Quraysh — the same clan as Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA). His father, Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, is one of the most remarkable figures of the pre-Islamic period: a man who, before the Prophet's ﷺ mission, rejected the idol worship of the Quraysh, refused to eat animals slaughtered in the name of idols, and traveled to Syria and elsewhere seeking the pure monotheistic religion of Ibrahim (AS). The Prophet ﷺ later testified: 'He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a nation by himself.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Manaqib al-Ansar). Zayd ibn Amr died before the formal onset of prophethood and thus died neither as a polytheist nor as a declared Muslim, a situation that classical scholars have discussed at length as a unique case.

Sa'id's connection to the early Islamic movement was intimate in two directions. His wife was Fatimah bint al-Khattab — the sister of Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA). It was at Sa'id and Fatimah's home that Umar famously came to confront his sister after hearing she had embraced Islam, only to hear the Quran recited and himself be moved to convert. The celebrated account of Umar's conversion, preserved in detail in Ibn Hisham's al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah, centers on this household. Sa'id and Fatimah had already accepted Islam before Umar, and their courage in the face of his initial violent reaction led directly to one of the most significant conversions in Islamic history.

Sa'id accepted Islam in the early Makkan period and endured persecution alongside the other early Muslims. He was among those who participated in the Hijrah to Madinah, and he fought in the major battles of the Prophet's ﷺ era. He participated in Badr, Uhud, al-Khandaq, Khaybar, the conquest of Makkah, and the Battle of Hunayn. Al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and Ibn Hajar in al-Isabah both confirm his presence in these campaigns.

During the great Islamic conquests following the Prophet's ﷺ death, Sa'id participated in campaigns in Syria (Sham). He was present at several of the major engagements in Syria under Abu Bakr and Umar. He served in a military capacity during the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman.

The hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ named him among the Ten Promised Paradise is one of the most authentic and well-known in the Sunnah: 'Abu Bakr is in Paradise, Umar is in Paradise, Uthman, Ali, Talha, Zubayr, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, Sa'id ibn Zayd, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas are in Paradise.' (Sunan Abi Dawud, Kitab al-Sunnah; al-Tirmidhi, Kitab al-Manaqib; graded sahih). This hadith is one of the primary bases for Sunni doctrine on the status of the senior Companions.

A well-known narration from Sa'id's later life involves a land dispute: a woman named Arwa bint Aws accused him of encroaching on her land. Sa'id denied it and called upon Allah to cause him to go blind if he was lying — according to various reports, he did subsequently lose his sight, though the cause-and-effect is recorded as part of the narrative by classical historians. Ibn Kathir discusses this in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah.

Sa'id died in 51 AH (671 CE), reportedly at his estate near Madinah. He is buried in the region of al-Aqiq. He narrated a modest number of hadith in the major collections.
